Hiring repeats the same job on you. A role trainer stops it.

Every new hire still pulls answers out of your head one question at a time.

A New Hire Trainer can teach one role from your own notes. Scripts and calls while you keep control.

Quick answer

Generic internet courses do not know your customers.

4 min read

  1. How to stop repeating basic role answers every time someone new starts
  2. Where a New Hire Trainer helps a new hire and where your sign-off stays

1You Are Still the Training Even After the Handbook

The problem

  1. New hires read a handbook.
  2. Still ask what to do for a client. What never to promise, or where to find a form. You hire for time back, spend the month sitting beside them. And pay for two people while getting one.

The way through

  1. Generic internet courses do not know your customers.
  2. Forms or exceptions, so you end up teaching it again. Put your real role rules in one place. A new starter can check approved notes first.

You hired for time back, not a full month of repeating yourself.

2Why Another Hire Does Not Fix It for you

The problem

  1. Another hire still needs your way of doing the job.
  2. So they pull it out of you one question at a time. Repeating what you already know is an easy trap,. Ignoring it leaves your next hire starting from zero.

The way through

  1. You write the job down once instead of re-explaining it every few months.
  2. Let a new person ask the notes before they interrupt you.

Ignoring your repeat loop just means the next hire starts from zero too.

3What your New Hire Trainer Does Inside the Business

The problem

  1. New starters get stuck on routine questions when you are busy.
  2. While existing staff also need clear company facts. Unchecked answers can drift if there is no clear boundary between a new starter's training path. Your rest of the team.

The way through

  1. Use a New Hire Trainer for one role using your scripts, notes.
  2. Calls, kept inside your business and never customer-facing. Point answers to approved notes. Leave gaps as questions if a note is silent. And keep broader team facts in a Company Brain.

The trainer is for someone who is new. Your Company Brain is for someone who already works here.

Free guide

If this sounds like your hiring month, get the AI Implementation Guide. Start with one role. Write that job down first.

4What Stays With You on Judgement and Sign-Off

The problem

  1. Awkward clients, edge cases.
  2. Unrecorded exceptions need human judgement that notes alone cannot settle. If your notes are wrong. A trainer built on them will teach your wrong job.

The way through

  1. You keep final say on what good looks like and sign off.
  2. New hires face a customer, a site or a regulator. Own and update your source notes yourself so the role stays accurate.

You still make the judgement calls, and you own the notes.

Ask for a quote

5You start With One Role and Measure the Days

The problem

  1. Trying to fix every role at once stalls. Your first hiring cycle even finishes.
  2. Without a baseline, it is hard to see whether onboarding is actually taking fewer days of your time.

The way through

  1. Pick the role you hire most often.
  2. You write the first week: common questions. Tasks they must not do alone yet. You write down how many days it takes before they work. You in the chair, both before and after.

You start with one role, write the first week down. And measure your days yourself.

If this sounds like your hiring month. Read your AI Implementation Guide first. You can map one role on paper before changing anything else. There is no rush to overhaul your whole business at once. And you start with a single role you already know well.
